strengths: Slide 1 creates a memorable request-packet premise with a glowing isometric portal/server scene, then slides 2–5 consistently trace that same login request through browser, API, application, database, bcrypt, and session state.
Slide 2 provides a recognizable browser form beside concrete 303 and 401 response cards rather than relying only on prose.

Slide 3 is the strongest information-design move in either deck: seven connected cards, directional arrows, colored trust boundaries, and an isometric infrastructure backdrop make the authentication sequence visible as a system.
Slide 5 clearly contrasts browser state with server state and explains regeneration as a five-step transition; this is well suited to a live B.Tech demonstration.
Slides 6–7 convert the architecture into a threat-control map and executable test plan, giving the presentation a practical laboratory ending rather than a generic summary.

strengths: Slides 1–2 establish a coherent terminal-inspired visual language, and slide 2 does include a recognizable login form plus request, success, and failure response panels.
Slide 4 uses syntax coloring and concise decision annotations to make validation, dummy-hash comparison, and generic rejection understandable.
Slide 5 is the deck's best explanatory composition: two rows of connected state cards distinguish session creation from the next authenticated request.
Slide 6 maps each named threat to a concrete control and outcome, while slide 7 turns those controls into a practical live-demo checklist.
The technical content across slides 1–7 is generally credible, explicitly illustrative, and avoids unsupported statistics or quotations.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 5's two-row session flow, connecting anonymous state, regenerate(), server storage, opaque cookie, and the subsequent dashboard request.

result.reason: Deck A is the deck to give the user. Its approximate weighted score is 3.85 versus 2.65 for B, and the preference is not order-sensitive. A visibly realizes the requested isometric architecture, browser UI, API cards, code, shield imagery, glow, and directional flow; B omits several of those required visual subjects and remains mostly a text-heavy terminal template. Both satisfy the exact seven-slide count, dark palette, technical audience, and core Student Authentication Portal subject, and neither shows harmful technical distortion or unsupported statistics. Neither is fully ready: A has a blocking cropped code slide, while B has multiple clipped slides and a blocking brief-fit failure. The most effective single improvement to B would be replacing the disconnected terminal grids with one persistent, arrow-connected isometric request-packet architecture. Route identity is unavailable, so the original arm cannot be identified; visually, the more complex A earns much of its complexity through slides 1–3 and 5, although slide 4 shows that the added complexity was not production-tested. A exceeds competent default quality in concept and visual specificity, but not yet in final rendering craft.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: Rebuild slide 4 as a complete, unclipped code-to-state transition and apply the same safe-margin discipline to slide 2. If the full success path visibly connects bcrypt comparison to regenerate(), server-side identity, Set-Cookie, and the 303 redirect, the strong opening, exceptional slide 3 trace, and practical slide 7 ending could support sustained rather than occasional wow.
